headline: Six big tech outages hit the U.S. in six days

chunks.text: Six big tech [[outages]] hit the U.S. in six days in November 2026. An outage is a time when a service stops working. The problems {{set off}} fears of a [[cyberattack]], an attack on computer systems by criminals or another country. Vice President Vance said friends asked if they should {{stock up on}} food and water. He said no. Officials and the companies said there was no [[evidence]] of an attack.

verbs.wrong: To report something on the news
verbs.why: Higher prices often set off angry complaints. One small mistake sets off a big argument. The six outages set off fears of a cyberattack.

verbs.correct: To buy a lot of something to keep
verbs.wrong: To sell something at a low price
verbs.why: Families stock up on water before a big storm. Many shoppers stock up on rice when it is on sale. Vance said friends asked if they should stock up on food and water.

chunks.text: On November 12, Microsoft's Outlook email and Teams, its program for online meetings, {{went down}} around the world. The company said its services {{came back}} on November 14. On November 13, the agency that runs U.S. air traffic stopped all [[departing flights]] for hours. Officials {{tracked the problem down}} to a [[faulty]] router, a device that moves data between computers.

verbs.correct: To stop working for a time
verbs.why: A website goes down when too many people visit it. Our office internet goes down almost every Monday. Microsoft's email and Teams went down around the world.

verbs.wrong: To be sold to a new owner
verbs.why: Our Wi-Fi comes back after a short break. The TV signal usually comes back when the rain stops. Microsoft's services came back on November 14.

verbs.correct: To find something by searching carefully
verbs.wrong: To return a broken thing to a store
verbs.why: Police track down the owner of a lost dog. She often tracks down old friends online. Officials tracked the problem down to a faulty router.

chunks.text: On November 16, thousands of Chase Bank customers reported trouble {{logging in}} to their [[online accounts]]. The bank said a [[software bug]], a mistake in computer code, {{slowed down}} payments. The trouble {{spilled over}} to other banks. A computer problem [[delayed]] United Airlines flights. On November 17, Apple said an [[internal update]] {{knocked out}} Apple Pay and other services. That day, a secret network at the National Security Agency, a U.S. [[spy agency]], stopped working.

verbs.correct: To enter a password to use an account
verbs.wrong: To close an account and open a new one
verbs.why: I log in to my email every morning. She logs in to the school website to check her grades. Thousands of Chase customers reported trouble logging in to their online accounts.

verbs.correct: To make something happen less quickly
verbs.wrong: To make something happen in secret
verbs.why: Heavy snow slows down traffic in the city. A weak signal slows down my phone. The bank said a software bug slowed down payments.

verbs.correct: To spread to other people or places
verbs.wrong: To be paid back to customers
verbs.why: Noise from a loud party spills over into the next apartment. Traffic on the highway often spills over onto small streets. The trouble at Chase spilled over to other banks.

verbs.wrong: To copy something to a new phone
verbs.why: A big storm often knocks out power to many homes. One broken cable knocks out the internet for a whole street. Apple said an internal update knocked out Apple Pay and other services.

chunks.text: On November 18, top [[security officials]] told Congress the outages were not connected. The head of the U.S. spy agencies said they came from [[routine maintenance]] and technical changes. Some [[lawmakers]] {{pushed back}} and asked for clearer answers. A day earlier, a senator who helps lead the Senate's spy agency committee said there was no sign of an attack. But he said artificial intelligence, or AI, now finds [[weak spots]] in software fast. He said pressure has {{built up}} to fix them quickly. Older systems cannot {{keep up with}} that [[pace]], he said.

verbs.correct: To show that you do not agree
verbs.wrong: To count the votes one more time
verbs.why: Workers push back when the boss asks for longer hours. Parents often push back against new school rules. Some lawmakers pushed back and asked for clearer answers.

verbs.correct: To slowly grow bigger or stronger
verbs.wrong: To be written into a law
verbs.why: Snow builds up on the roof in winter. Stress builds up when work never stops. The senator said pressure has built up to fix weak spots quickly.

verbs.correct: To go as fast as something else
verbs.wrong: To cost the same as something else
verbs.why: Slow walkers cannot keep up with the tour group. Her son runs to keep up with her on walks. The senator said older systems cannot keep up with that pace.

wordDefs.def: Times when a service, such as power or the internet, stops working
ex: Power outages are common here in the summer.
The phone company apologized for the outages.
We keep candles at home for outages.

wordDefs.def: An attack on computers or networks by criminals or another country
ex: The hospital lost its records in a cyberattack.
A cyberattack closed the city's website for two days.
Strong passwords help protect a company from a cyberattack.

wordDefs.def: Facts that show something is true
ex: The police found new evidence in the case.
There is no evidence that the drink is unhealthy.
Do you have any evidence for that idea?

wordDefs.def: Government workers whose job is to keep a country safe
ex: Security officials warned of a new threat to the country.
The president met with top security officials.
Security officials said the border was safe.

wordDefs.def: Planes that are leaving an airport
ex: The screen lists all departing flights.
Fog delayed many departing flights this morning.
Departing flights leave from the second floor.

wordDefs.def: Not working the way it should
ex: The store replaced my faulty phone charger.
A faulty wire started the fire.
The car had a faulty brake light.

wordDefs.def: Personal spaces on websites that you open with a name and password
ex: Use a different password for each of your online accounts.
My grandmother has three online accounts for shopping.
Check your online accounts for strange activity.

wordDefs.def: A mistake in a computer program that makes it work badly
ex: A software bug made the game freeze.
The company fixed the software bug in a day.
One small software bug can cause big problems.
Heavy snow delayed our train.
The meeting was delayed by an hour.
Traffic delayed the delivery truck.

wordDefs.def: A change a company makes to its own systems
ex: The website was slow after an internal update.
Our team planned an internal update for Sunday night.
An internal update changed how the office email works.

wordDefs.def: A government office that collects secret information
ex: Her uncle worked for a spy agency for many years.
The movie is about a young woman at a spy agency.
Every large country has at least one spy agency.

wordDefs.def: Regular planned work to keep machines or systems in good condition
ex: The pool is closed for routine maintenance.
Routine maintenance keeps the elevators safe.
The website will be down tonight for routine maintenance.

wordDefs.def: People who make laws, such as members of Congress
ex: Lawmakers voted on the new budget.
Parents asked lawmakers to make the roads safer.
State lawmakers met with teachers.

wordDefs.def: Parts of something that can be easily harmed or attacked
ex: The coach studies the other team's weak spots.
Old windows are weak spots in a cold house.
Testing helps find weak spots in a plan.

wordDefs.def: The speed at which something happens
ex: Prices are rising at a fast pace.
She runs at a steady pace.
The pace of work slows in August.

mainIdea.s: In six days, failures at tech companies, banks, airlines and a spy agency made many Americans fear hackers. Officials found no sign of an attack and said the problems were not connected.
mainIdea.why: The outages set off fears of a cyberattack. Officials told Congress there was no sign of one, and the outages were not connected.

mainIdea.s: Six computer failures in six days made many Americans fear an attack by hackers. Officials told Congress the failures were all connected and came from one faulty update at a tech company.
mainIdea.why: Close, but officials said the outages were not connected. Each had its own cause, such as a software bug or routine maintenance.

mainIdea.s: A new law will make U.S. banks and airlines test their computer systems for problems once a month. Congress passed it after a long debate over the cost of these regular safety checks.
mainIdea.why: No new law was passed. Six tech outages hit the U.S., and they set off fears of a cyberattack.

tf.s: The six outages set off fears of a cyberattack.
tf.why: Many people worried that criminals or another country had attacked U.S. computer systems.

tf.s: Apple said a cyberattack knocked out its services.
tf.why: Apple said an internal update knocked out Apple Pay and other services.

tf.s: Chase said a software bug slowed down its payments.
tf.why: The bank said a mistake in computer code, not an attack, slowed down payments.

tf.s: Officials told Congress that the six outages were all connected.
tf.why: Officials said each outage had its own cause. Apple, for example, said an update knocked out its services.

tf.s: Some lawmakers pushed back and asked officials for clearer answers.
tf.why: After officials spoke to Congress, some lawmakers pushed back and asked for clearer answers.

tf.s: A senator said there were clear signs of an attack.
tf.why: The senator said there was no sign of an attack. He said pressure has built up to fix weak spots quickly.

lines.text: Did you hear about all the tech outages? Six in six days.
I did. First Microsoft email {{went down}}, then the flights stopped.
And then Chase. My sister had trouble {{logging in}} to her account.
The bank says no. It said a software bug {{slowed down}} payments.
So all six were [[just a coincidence]]?
That's what officials told Congress. They say the outages weren't connected.
Still, it [[makes me nervous]]. Some people asked if they should {{stock up on}} food and water.
I understand why. The outages {{set off}} a lot of fears.
Apple said an update {{knocked out}} Apple Pay and other services for a few hours.
[[It happens]], I guess. Big systems are complicated.
[[At least]] most of the services {{came back}} within a day or two.
Yes. Some lawmakers wanted clearer answers. One senator says AI is adding pressure.
AI caused all of this? [[I'm not so sure about that]].
He didn't say that. He said older systems can't {{keep up with}} how fast AI finds weak spots.

expressions.def: Used when two things happen together by chance, not for a reason
ex: We both wore red shirts today. It's just a coincidence.

expressions.def: Used to say that something makes you feel worried
ex: Driving in heavy snow makes me nervous.

expressions.def: Used to say that a problem is normal and not too serious
ex: "Sorry, I broke a glass." "It happens. Don't worry."

expressions.def: Used to point out one good thing in a bad situation
ex: I missed the bus, but at least it was not raining.

expressions.expr: I'm not so sure about that
expressions.def: Used to say politely that you doubt what someone said
ex: "This movie will win every prize." "I'm not so sure about that."
